article_title: Space: The Misguided Promise of Privatization
news_headline: SpaceX's AI Splurge Puts Damper on Debut Earnings After IPO
post_text:
SpaceX went public in June at $135 a share, briefly touched $225, then fell apart. By the time its first earnings report landed August 4, the stock had erased over $1 trillion in market value from its peak. The results themselves were strong on paper: $7.8 billion in Q2 revenue, up 92% year-over-year. But capital expenditures hit $28.5 billion in just the first half of 2026, more than four times the prior-year pace, and the company reported a $541 million net loss. Shares dropped another 8% after hours.

This is the central tension in the SpaceX story: a genuine engineering operation now dressed in the clothes of a high-multiple tech stock, asked to justify a valuation built on narrative as much as fundamentals. The gap between IPO euphoria and cash-burn reality is widening fast.

WBR's piece on the misguided promise of space privatization argued exactly this, that the romantic commercial framing obscures how dependent these ventures remain on government contracts, public infrastructure, and capital markets willing to absorb years of losses. SpaceX's debut quarter as a public company is a real-time stress test of that argument. The article is on our site.
